explainedBy: The brain's energy allocation is compared to a city's power grid.

storyboard.claim: Leveling up ignores homeostasis' dark side: the brain allocates energy like a city grid.
storyboard.concreteVisual: A city icon alone: the grid the analogy is built on.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Answers the hope that a built brain stays built.
storyboard.addedInformation: The city sets up the power-grid analogy before it is explained.

explainedBy: Cause -> effect: when the factory closes, the city cuts its power to save resources.

storyboard.claim: A city stops powering an abandoned factory to save resources.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Flow: factory shuts down -> power cut off.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Plays out the city-grid analogy.
storyboard.addedInformation: The cause -> effect of the analogy, which the brain will copy.

explainedBy: Retired cabbies who stopped driving London lost their enlarged hippocampi.

storyboard.claim: Retired London cabbies saw their enlarged hippocampi shrink back to normal once they stopped navigating.
storyboard.concreteVisual: The cabbie slumped beside his black cab, no longer driving.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: The analogy proven on real people.
storyboard.addedInformation: Shows who lost the growth and why (they stopped driving the cab).

explainedBy: Cause -> effect: stop demanding peak capacity and the brain tears down the extra gray matter.

storyboard.claim: If you stop pushing at the edge, the brain tears down extra gray matter to save energy.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Flow: stop pushing -> gray matter torn down.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Generalizes the cabbie finding into the rule.
storyboard.addedInformation: The mechanism of the loss, step by step.

explainedBy: The same flow ends in the rule: use it or lose it, never permanently leveled up.

storyboard.claim: It's use it or lose it at a cellular level; you are never permanently leveled up.
storyboard.concreteVisual: The kept flow gains its last step: lose it.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Kept flow; adds the third label "Lose it".
storyboard.addedInformation: Names the result of the mechanism: the gain is lost.

explainedBy: A comfortable person sitting back while the brain stops improving: comfort ends the gains.

storyboard.claim: The moment you get comfortable, the brain dismantles the scaffolding; comfort is where improvement stops.
storyboard.concreteVisual: The everyman sits back contentedly beside the brain icon.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: From the mechanism to the everyday trap.
storyboard.addedInformation: weak: the comfort is visible, the dismantling only in the callout.

explainedBy: The physical brain changes create a psychological software: hardware -> software.

storyboard.claim: From the physical hardware changes in the brain to the psychological software they create.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Flow: brain hardware -> psychological software.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Closes the brain-growth section, opens the next.
storyboard.addedInformation: Shows the chapter turn as a structure.

explainedBy: The brain icon labelled as the true secret: the mechanism of expert performance.

storyboard.claim: This software is the true secret of expert performance, the mechanism of genius.
storyboard.concreteVisual: The brain icon alone with the label.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Announces the payoff of the turn just made.
storyboard.addedInformation: weak: a teaser line; the brain marks it as a mental mechanism.

explainedBy: 1924, Hotel Alamac: the chess grandmaster before his blindfold exhibition.

storyboard.claim: April 1924, the Hotel Alamac in New York City.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Alekhine in his 1924 suit walks into the hotel room.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Opens the Alekhine story.
storyboard.addedInformation: Time and place, with the man the scene is about.

explainedBy: Alekhine sinks into a chair and stares blankly: he is not looking at any board.

storyboard.claim: The grandmaster Alekhine sinks into a leather chair, staring blankly at a wall.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Alekhine sits down, blank-faced.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Kept stage; he now sits with a blank face.
storyboard.addedInformation: His posture shows he looks at nothing.

explainedBy: The chessboards he cannot see appear beside the seated, blank-faced Alekhine.

storyboard.claim: Behind him are 26 chess boards; he cannot see a single one.
storyboard.concreteVisual: The chessboard appears beside the seated Alekhine who does not look at it.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Kept stage; adds the chessboard.
storyboard.addedInformation: The boards and the man who cannot see them, in one frame.

explainedBy: The runner calls out a move and Alekhine calls back a counter-move without looking.

storyboard.claim: A runner yells a move from board seven; Alekhine instantly calls back a counter-move.
storyboard.concreteVisual: The messenger calls the move; Alekhine answers from his chair.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Kept stage; the runner enters and the exchange begins.
storyboard.addedInformation: Shows how the blind game works: moves by voice.

explainedBy: Alekhine plays all 26 games in his head: the brain replaces the boards beside him.

storyboard.claim: He plays 26 simultaneous games against strong opponents entirely in his mind.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Alekhine keeps answering, the brain icon in place of the boards; the runner is amazed.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Kept stage; the chessboard becomes the brain.
storyboard.addedInformation: The games live in his head, not on a board.

explainedBy: Ericsson rejects the idea that experts simply have better, faster memory.

storyboard.claim: It looks like magic, but experts do not just have better memory; they see a different reality.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Ericsson explains beside the brain, the memory claim struck out.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: The researcher explains the feat just shown.
storyboard.addedInformation: Marks the rejected explanation.

explainedBy: Cause -> effect: thousands of hours of deliberate practice build mental representations.

storyboard.claim: Through thousands of hours of deliberate practice they build sophisticated mental representations.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Flow: deliberate practice -> mental representations.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Answers "how do they see it differently?"
storyboard.addedInformation: Names the mechanism and its cause.

explainedBy: An amateur looks at a chessboard and sees only 32 carved pieces of wood.

storyboard.claim: Representations bypass short-term memory; to an amateur a chessboard is just 32 pieces on 64 squares.
storyboard.concreteVisual: The everyman blank-faced beside the chessboard.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Sets up the amateur side of the contrast.
storyboard.addedInformation: The amateur's flat view of the board.

explainedBy: Comparison: the amateur sees pieces on a board; Alekhine sees a web of lines of force and weaknesses.

storyboard.claim: To Alekhine the board is a dynamic web of lines of force and structural weaknesses.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Sorter: amateur sees pieces, Alekhine sees lines of force.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Completes the amateur vs expert contrast.
storyboard.addedInformation: Both readings of the same board side by side.

explainedBy: The confident mechanic next to a man who knows nothing about cars: the two sides of the analogy.

storyboard.claim: An analogy: a seasoned auto mechanic versus someone who knows nothing about cars.
storyboard.concreteVisual: The veteran mechanic beside the anxious everyman in a garage.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: A new analogy for a mental representation.
storyboard.addedInformation: Introduces the expert and the novice who will hear the same noise.

noVisual: No engine or car icon in the vocabulary; the noise is carried by the face and the callout.
explainedBy: The novice hears the clanking engine and only feels fear.

storyboard.claim: When my engine clanks, I just hear loud scary noise.
storyboard.concreteVisual: The everyman flinches, afraid.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Kept stage; the novice reacts.
storyboard.addedInformation: The novice has no structure, only fear.

explainedBy: The mechanic hears the same noise and calmly points to its cause while the novice is still afraid.

storyboard.claim: A veteran mechanic hears the same sound and his brain generates a high-definition image.
storyboard.concreteVisual: The mechanic points confidently; the novice is still afraid.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Kept stage; now the expert reacts to the same noise.
storyboard.addedInformation: Same input, two different reactions.

explainedBy: Mechanism: the representation translates the raw noise into its meaning, a worn-out belt.

storyboard.claim: He pictures a worn serpentine belt slapping a loose pulley; the representation turns raw data into structure.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Flow: clanking noise -> mental representation -> worn-out belt.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Explains what happened inside the mechanic.
storyboard.addedInformation: The translation step the analogy is about.

explainedBy: The expert sees the whole forest while the novice stares at the leaves.

storyboard.claim: They see the forest; I am stuck staring at the leaves. The same happens with diagnosticians.
storyboard.concreteVisual: The tree beside the confident mechanic and the dejected novice.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Sums up the mechanic analogy.
storyboard.addedInformation: weak: the tree labels the forest image; the faces carry who sees it.

explainedBy: A patient in the emergency room with confusing symptoms.

storyboard.claim: A patient arrives with vague symptoms: dizziness, a slight eye droop and neck pain.
storyboard.concreteVisual: The patient slumps in his gown, worried.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: New case: medicine.
storyboard.addedInformation: Lists the symptoms on the person who has them.

explainedBy: The novice resident, lost in her checklist, over the waiting patient.

storyboard.claim: A first-year resident gets lost in a massive linear checklist.
storyboard.concreteVisual: The resident slumps over her notes while the patient waits.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Kept stage; the novice doctor enters.
storyboard.addedInformation: Shows the novice method: a list held in hand.

explainedBy: The expert diagnostician recognizes the pattern at once and points to it.

storyboard.claim: An expert diagnostician immediately recognizes a high-level pattern; a rare case is detailed.
storyboard.concreteVisual: The diagnostician points at the patient with a lightbulb: recognized.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Kept stage; the expert replaces the resident.
storyboard.addedInformation: Novice vs expert on the same patient.

explainedBy: The expert tells the patient the rare diagnosis: a torn carotid artery.

storyboard.claim: She diagnosed a rare torn carotid artery, not by connecting symptoms one by one.
storyboard.concreteVisual: The diagnostician delivers the diagnosis; the patient is surprised.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Kept stage; from recognition to diagnosis.
storyboard.addedInformation: Names the rare diagnosis she reached.

explainedBy: Mechanism: the symptoms are matched against an if-then pattern held in her head.

storyboard.claim: They mapped the presentation against a complex if-then pattern held in their head.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Flow: symptoms -> if-then pattern.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Explains how the diagnosis was reached.
storyboard.addedInformation: The representation as a step between data and answer.

explainedBy: The same flow reaches its end: the pattern lets them jump straight to the correct conclusion.

storyboard.claim: The representation lets them jump straight to the correct conclusion. Could Alekhine just have photographic memory?
storyboard.concreteVisual: The kept flow gains its last step: correct conclusion.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Kept flow; adds "Correct conclusion".
storyboard.addedInformation: The result of the mechanism.

explainedBy: The objection: maybe Alekhine just takes a photo of each board in his head.

storyboard.claim: Maybe his brain just takes a high-resolution mental Polaroid of the 26 boards.
storyboard.concreteVisual: The everyman holds up a photo, the objection made literal.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Raises the counter-theory.
storyboard.addedInformation: The photo shows what the objection claims memory is.

explainedBy: Still holding the photo: why not just call it a freakishly good visual memory?

storyboard.claim: Pulling them up like a JPEG; why not just a freakishly good visual memory?
storyboard.concreteVisual: The everyman keeps the photo, now with a challenging smirk.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Kept stage; the face turns to a challenge.
storyboard.addedInformation: weak: the challenge is in the face; the photo stays the claim.

explainedBy: Herbert Simon's chess study dismantled the photographic memory theory.

storyboard.claim: The photographic memory theory was dismantled by Herbert Simon's 1970s chess study.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Simon points at the chessboard; the theory is struck out.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Answers the objection.
storyboard.addedInformation: Who refuted it and with what (the chessboard).

explainedBy: Simon times a grandmaster looking at a board for exactly 5 seconds.

storyboard.claim: Simon showed grandmasters and novices a chess board for exactly 5 seconds.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Simon with a stopwatch, the grandmaster as the subject.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Kept stage; the experiment begins.
storyboard.addedInformation: Shows the timed test and who took it.

explainedBy: Comparison: on real game positions grandmasters recall almost everything, novices three or four pieces.

storyboard.claim: With real game positions, grandmasters recreated the board almost perfectly; novices remembered three or four pieces.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Sorter: grandmasters almost perfect vs novices 3 or 4 pieces.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: The first result of the experiment.
storyboard.addedInformation: The size of the expert gap.

explainedBy: Simon scrambles the pieces at random, against the rules of chess, for the grandmaster.

storyboard.claim: Then Simon arranged the pieces randomly, violating all the logic of chess.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Simon points at the board, a knowing look; the grandmaster waits.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: The twist of the experiment.
storyboard.addedInformation: Shows who changes the board and for whom.

explainedBy: On the random board the grandmaster is lost: no better than the novices.

storyboard.claim: The grandmasters' memory was suddenly no better than the novices'.
storyboard.concreteVisual: The grandmaster slumps, surprised, at the random board.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Kept stage; the grandmaster now reacts.
storyboard.addedInformation: The expert advantage disappears on screen.

explainedBy: Comparison: they were not memorizing pieces of wood; they were recognizing patterns of force.

storyboard.claim: They were not memorizing pieces of wood but recognizing meaningful patterns of force and strategy.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Sorter: pieces of wood vs patterns of force.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Explains the random-board result.
storyboard.addedInformation: What experts actually store.

explainedBy: Without the logical pattern the grandmaster's superpower vanished.

storyboard.claim: When the logical pattern was removed, their superpower vanished entirely.
storyboard.concreteVisual: The grandmaster slumps sadly beside the board.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: The consequence of the mechanism.
storyboard.addedInformation: The expert without his advantage.

explainedBy: Not photographic memory: highly specific, domain-dependent representations in the brain.

storyboard.claim: They didn't have photographic memories but domain-dependent mental representations.
storyboard.concreteVisual: The brain icon with the conclusion.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: States the conclusion of the study.
storyboard.addedInformation: weak: the brain marks the mind; the label carries the term.

callout.text: the very edge of its capability

explainedBy: A person straining at the limit of what his brain can do: the condition that forges representations.

storyboard.claim: Those representations are forged only when the brain struggles at the edge of its capability.
storyboard.concreteVisual: The everyman strains, worried, beside the brain.
storyboard.onScreenText: the very edge of its capability
storyboard.relationToPrevious: From what representations are to how they are built.
storyboard.addedInformation: The struggle shown on a person.

explainedBy: Comparison: coasting through easy games builds nothing; analyzing where your logic failed builds the representation.

storyboard.claim: You don't build a representation by coasting through easy games but by analyzing where your logic failed.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Sorter: coasting through easy games vs where your logic failed.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Spells out the struggle from the previous beat.
storyboard.addedInformation: The two ways of practicing side by side.

explainedBy: The host raises a cultural idea that distorted how time and practice relate.

storyboard.claim: The elephant in the room: a cultural phenomenon that distorted how time and practice relate.
storyboard.concreteVisual: The host, concerned, beside a clock.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Turns to the next topic.
storyboard.addedInformation: weak: a teaser; the clock marks time spent practicing.
